article_title: Function Art: Understanding the Artistic Transformation of Mathematical Functions through Learning Analytics
citation: Bautista, G. Jr., Cacuyong, R., Lavicza, Z., Sabitzer, B., & Emara, M. (2026). Function Art: Understanding the Artistic Transformation of Mathematical Functions through Learning Analytics. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.9037
title: Three types of function art: pure, organic, and hybrid
description: The article categorizes function art into three types based on how mathematical functions are used in artistic expression. Pure function art consists solely of function graphs (e.g., linear, quadratic, sine). Organic function art primarily uses functions but incorporates mathematical objects such as conics when needed. Hybrid function art blends functions with geometric primitives, image overlays, and annotations. Classification rules distinguish organic from hybrid based on whether functions were used whenever possible.
requirements: Classification requires examining whether curves could have been achieved with functions but the student chose not to use them
constraints: Circles and vertical line segments cannot be straightforwardly represented as functions in GeoGebra, so artworks using only these alongside functions are classified as organic
target_learners: Grades 8-12 mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Understanding function families and their graphical representations
Distinguishing between function-based and non-function-based mathematical objects
examples: Artworks using only functions and circles were classified as organic; artworks including arcs that fail the vertical line test were classified as organic; artworks with general line segments, polygons, or imported images were classified as hybrid
key_sources: Bautista, G. Jr., Cacuyong, R., Lavicza, Z., Sabitzer, B., & Emara, M. (2026). Function Art: Understanding the Artistic Transformation of Mathematical Functions through Learning Analytics. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.9037
grain_size: task-level taxonomy for classifying student-created mathematical artworks

article_title: Preparing Early Childhood Teachers: Credentialing and Preparation Programs in Four States
citation: Schachner, A., Wang, V., Yun, C., Plasencia, S., Mauerman, C., McJunkins, C., & Stipek, D. (2025). Preparing early childhood teachers: Credentialing and preparation programs in four states. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/177.512
title: Sustained, intensive supervised clinical placements with mentorship and reflection strengthen early childhood teaching practice
description: A program-level design pattern in which candidates complete sustained and intensive supervised clinical experiences, ideally full-year placements, with strong mentorship and individual and group reflection opportunities. The report's research summary states that "Providing sustained and intensive supervised clinical experiences, such as full-year supervised clinical placements with strong mentorship and opportunities for reflection individually and in groups, strengthens practice." Required clinical length varies across the four study states from one semester to a full year, with Louisiana requiring a full-year placement.
requirements: Strong mentorship and opportunities for reflection individually and in groups
Partnerships with schools that instantiate best practices and provide a well-supported setting to learn to teach
constraints: State clinical requirements vary from one semester to a full year; Massachusetts and New York allow prior classroom experience to count toward clinical requirements
target_learners: early childhood teacher credential candidates
target_learning_goals: application of child development knowledge in clinical settings
examples: Louisiana requires a 1-year, full-time clinical placement for its PreK–3 credential; New York requires 70 days plus 100 hours of field experience for candidates entering in fall 2024 or later

article_title: Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System
citation: Jen DeNeal, Emily Hatch & Bradley Kingston. (2023). Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System. The Education Trust-Midwest. https://edtrustmidwest.org
title: Fully fund the foundation allowance for students with disabilities and close the special education shortfall gap
description: The brief recommends Michigan provide districts the full foundation allowance for students with disabilities plus reimbursements for special education delivery, prioritizing closure of the "shortfall gap" between district spending and state reimbursement. Michigan currently provides only 75% of the foundation allowance for these students and reimburses just over 28% of special education service costs.
requirements: Replacing the partial reimbursement system under which districts shoulder much of the funding responsibility
Lawmakers should investigate options for creating a weighted funding formula for students with disabilities
constraints: One early-2023 estimate put the shortfall gap at $343 million; cited research suggests adequately funding students with disabilities may require weights of at least 185% of base funding
target_learners: students with disabilities
peers without disabilities in underfunded districts
target_learning_goals: access to needed special education services and supports
examples: Michigan's fiscal year 2023 budget invested deeply in closing the shortfall gap, which the brief calls a first step toward funding equity
key_sources: Jen DeNeal, Emily Hatch & Bradley Kingston. (2023). Eliminating the Opportunity Gaps: Creating a Truly Fair and Equitable Funding System. The Education Trust-Midwest. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED630507

article_title: Evaluating Scaffolding-Oriented Multi-Agent Large Language Model System for Clinical Interview Training
citation: Yang, L., Liu, H., Li, S., Jia, R., Xiao, Y., Chen, G., & Lu, L. (2026). Evaluating Scaffolding-Oriented Multi-Agent Large Language Model System for Clinical Interview Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10939
title: Functional complementarity model of AI and human roles in clinical skills education
description: The article proposes that AI and human educators need not perform identical instructional work: "AI agents may be especially useful for repetitive practice, consistent role-play, checklist monitoring, Socratic prompting, and the generation of preliminary formative feedback," while faculty and human standardized patients contribute contextual interpretation, nuanced emotional response, individualized remediation, and judgments about learner readiness. On this account, partial substitution is acceptable only for specific, bounded tasks, with the boundary set by error consequences, task uncertainty, relational sensitivity, and availability of human review.
requirements: meaningful human review of consequential judgments
AI systems that scaffold rather than substitute student reasoning
constraints: the system should not autonomously determine whether a learner is clinically competent, make progression or credentialing decisions, or replace human-led remediation in emotionally or professionally complex cases
target_learners: medical students in early clinical training
examples: The authors suggest an AI-SP may substitute for some repetitive early-stage interview practice and an evaluator agent may provide preliminary checklist-coverage feedback
key_sources: Yang, L., Liu, H., Li, S., Jia, R., Xiao, Y., Chen, G., & Lu, L. (2026). Evaluating Scaffolding-Oriented Multi-Agent Large Language Model System for Clinical Interview Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10939

article_title: AI in inclusive education: teachers’ visions of future-oriented practices
citation: Daniusevičiūtė-Brazaitė L, Gaižiūnienė L and Pučėtaitė R (2026) AI in inclusive education: teachers' visions of future-oriented practices. Front. Educ. 11:1890925. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1890925
title: Futures thinking as a dimension of teacher agency and professional competence for AI-driven inclusive education
description: The article integrates Emirbayer and Mische's temporal agency model (iterative, practical-evaluative, projective dimensions) with futures thinking and the Future Scaffolding Skills Framework of Barelli et al. (2022) to analyze teachers' visions. It argues that "futures thinking functions as a bridge between current practice and educational transformation rather than as a purely aspirational exercise". The framework positions teachers not just as technology users but as active agents shaping inclusive educational futures.
requirements: Teachers need opportunities to envision alternative future scenarios and connect them to present possibilities for action
constraints: The framework was applied in the Lithuanian context where inclusive education policy intersects with AI adoption; findings are not statistically generalizable
target_learners: high school teachers
target_learning_goals: envisioning and negotiating AI-supported inclusive educational change
examples: 50 teachers wrote essays envisioning themselves in 2040 in AI-rich learning environments, analyzed deductively with the Future Scaffolding Skills Framework
key_sources: Daniusevičiūtė-Brazaitė L, Gaižiūnienė L and Pučėtaitė R (2026) AI in inclusive education: teachers' visions of future-oriented practices. Front. Educ. 11:1890925. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1890925

article_title: GenAI dependence and graduate students’ research creativity: the roles of critical thinking and human–AI collaboration quality
citation: Yin S, Wu R, Liu X and Li R (2026) GenAI dependence and graduate students' research creativity: the roles of critical thinking and human–AI collaboration quality. Front. Psychol. 17:1896963. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1896963
title: Differentiated two-dimensional conceptualization of GenAI dependence: functional versus existential dependence
description: The article conceptualizes graduate students' GenAI dependence as two qualitatively distinct dimensions rather than a unitary construct. Functional dependence "refers to the instrumental and task-oriented use of GenAI to support speciﬁc academic or research-related activities," whereas existential dependence "refers to a deeper psychological and cognitive reliance on GenAI, in which individuals may feel less conﬁdent or less capable of completing research tasks independently without AI assistance." Functional dependence is described as an objective behavioral-level description and existential dependence as deep psychological involvement, drawing on the AI Dependence Questionnaire of Li et al. (2025) and Extended Mind Theory. The study uses this distinction to show differentiated associations with research creativity.
requirements: Measurement via the 18-item two-dimension AI Dependence Questionnaire rated on a 5-point Likert scale
constraints: The distinction is grounded in scale-development research by Li et al. (2025) as cited by the article; associations are cross-sectional and associative rather than causal
target_learners: graduate students
target_learning_goals: self-directed AI use in academic research
examples: The study modeled functional and existential dependence as separate independent variables in parallel PROCESS Model 6 mediation models and compared their total and indirect effects
key_sources: Yin S, Wu R, Liu X and Li R (2026) GenAI dependence and graduate students' research creativity: the roles of critical thinking and human–AI collaboration quality. Front. Psychol. 17:1896963. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1896963

article_title: GenAI and AI tools for STEAM educators: evidence-informed strategies and resources for the future of teaching
citation: Dahal N, Hasan MK and Islam MT (2026). GenAI and AI tools for STEAM educators: evidence-informed strategies and resources for the future of teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1948064. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1948064
title: Functional five-category classification of AI and GenAI tools organized by what educators are trying to accomplish
description: Rather than classifying tools by technical capability, the review proposes an educator-centered functional classification: "a more useful classification centers on what educators are trying to accomplish: generate content, design instruction, provide assessment and feedback, interpret learning data, or support collaboration and creativity." Table 2 maps each category to representative examples, STEAM uses, pedagogical strengths, and common limitations. The review notes the listed tools are representative examples for pedagogical illustration, not endorsements.
requirements: Classification should be used for classroom planning around pedagogical functions rather than marketed technical capabilities
constraints: Inclusion of a tool in the classification does not imply endorsement or validated superiority
target_learners: STEAM educators planning classroom integration
target_learning_goals: tool selection aligned with pedagogical goals
examples: Table 2 lists Gradescope, Quizizz AI, and Kahoot AI under assessment and feedback tools, and PhET, GeoGebra, Wolfram Alpha, and Tinkercad under collaboration and creativity tools
key_sources: Dahal N, Hasan MK and Islam MT (2026). GenAI and AI tools for STEAM educators: evidence-informed strategies and resources for the future of teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1948064. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1948064

article_title: Exploring the Value of Diverse LLM Explanations in Introductory Programming
citation: Seth Bernstein, Paul Denny, Juho Leinonen, Kush Patel, Rayhona Nasimova, Matt Littlefield, and Stephen MacNeil. (2026). Exploring the Value of Diverse LLM Explanations in Introductory Programming. SIGCSE Virtual '26. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28882
title: Three-dimension semantic diversity framework for LLM code explanations (function, concept, goal)
description: The article operationalizes explanation diversity as three distinct semantic dimensions drawn from prior work on code comprehension: function, concept, and goal. In the Diverse condition, "we issued three distinct prompts targeting function, concept, and goal as the three dimensions, generating one explanation per dimension." These dimensions were chosen because prior work identifies them as distinct cognitive registers: "understanding what code does, why the underlying mechanism works, and what the program is trying to accomplish." Generic explanations, by contrast, were produced by issuing the identical prompt three times, covering the snippet in an all-purpose way. The framework is grounded in Variation Theory, which holds that learners grasp a concept when they see systematic variation exposing its critical features.
requirements: GPT-4o (or similar LLM) used to generate one explanation per dimension with distinct prompts targeting function, concept, and goal
constraints: The authors note the sources of variation employed may not have been aligned with the dimensions students needed to discern, and the study did not compare outcomes across the three explanation dimensions individually
target_learners: first-year computing students learning recursion in C
target_learning_goals: code comprehension and understanding of recursion concepts
examples: Students saw three explanations per snippet from one condition only: either three generic plain-text summaries or three dimension-targeted explanations (function, concept, goal)

article_title: 'Stuck in a Spiral": Shame and Guilt as Social Regulators of AI Use in Computing Education'
citation: Kate Hamilton, Irene Hou, Dev Patel, Sheena Nnam, Hena Patel, and Stephen MacNeil. (2026). “Stuck in a Spiral”: Shame and Guilt as Social Regulators of AI Use in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14920
title: Functionalist perspective of shame and guilt as social signals regulating behavior
description: The article adopts a functionalist perspective of social emotions, which "conceptualizes emotions as adaptive regulators of behavior in social contexts." Within this framing, guilt is oriented toward a specific behavior and motivates reparative action, whereas shame is oriented toward the self and elicits withdrawal, concealment, or identity threat. The framework guided the interview protocol and inductive coding, focusing on how students evaluated their behaviors and identities in relation to AI use, while remaining open to unanticipated patterns.
requirements: Applied via semi-structured interviews that avoid directly asking about specific emotions, letting emotional experiences emerge through students' own accounts
constraints: The article notes the functionalist lens may not fully capture the identity aspects uncovered in the findings
target_learners: undergraduate computing students
target_learning_goals: understanding socio-emotional regulation of AI use in coursework
examples: The study used the lens to interpret hiding behaviors, selective disclosure, shaming, and cycles of use among 19 computing students
key_sources: Kate Hamilton, Irene Hou, Dev Patel, Sheena Nnam, Hena Patel, and Stephen MacNeil. (2026). “Stuck in a Spiral”: Shame and Guilt as Social Regulators of AI Use in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14920

article_title: Artificial intelligence in educational leadership: a comprehensive taxonomy and future directions
citation: Martin Sposato. (2025). Artificial intelligence in educational leadership: a comprehensive taxonomy and future directions. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00517-1
title: Future-trends framework: five core trends shaping AI in educational leadership
description: Table 2 of the article maps five core future trends and their implications: AI-augmented decision making, advanced personalized learning, evolution of work roles, privacy and data ethics, and equity considerations. Each trend is paired with a primary impact, key challenges, and opportunities—for instance, AI-augmented decision making promises enhanced data-driven leadership but requires "Balancing AI insights with human judgment." The article frames these as developments leaders must prepare for, including possible new roles such as AI Ethics Officers or Educational Data Scientists.
requirements: Educational leaders will need to manage transitions so that AI complements rather than replaces human expertise
constraints: The article frames these as potential future directions, not established findings; it notes open questions about balancing AI-driven insights with human judgment and about AI widening existing gaps
target_learners: educational leaders
policymakers
target_learning_goals: anticipating and governing AI-driven change in educational institutions
examples: Table 2 pairs the equity trend with the challenge of ensuring AI does not widen existing gaps and the opportunity of more inclusive educational experiences
key_sources: Martin Sposato. (2025). Artificial intelligence in educational leadership: a comprehensive taxonomy and future directions. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00517-1

article_title: Reimagining teacher-AI co-design in learning task design: trends and perspectives
citation: Zongran Wang, Liu Mingzhuo & A.Y.M. Atiquil Islam. (2026). Reimagining teacher-AI co-design in learning task design: trends and perspectives. HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES COMMUNICATIONS. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06981-y
title: Functional-affordance framework of teacher-AI co-design: efficiency, responsiveness, creativity, and equity as interdependent dimensions
description: The review proposes a framework in which AI tools are selected for four pedagogical affordances: efficiency, responsiveness, creativity, and equity. The review states "this study identified four recurrent affordance types as efficiency, responsiveness, creativity, and equity, which reflect how AI functionality intervenes in core aspects of design." The affordances are conceptualized as interacting levers: "the four identified affordances do not function as isolated features but as interdependent dimensions of teacher–AI co-design." The framework reframes AI as a co-agent that reorganizes the temporal, cognitive, and relational structures of teaching, and can serve as a diagnostic tool for identifying overreliance on narrow AI functions.
requirements: Requires analysis of how specific AI features afford solutions to teachers' design problems such as reducing workload, responding to student variability, enriching content, or promoting inclusivity
constraints: The synthesis reveals a concentration of use around specific GenAI functions, especially prompt generation and scenario simulation, risking narrowing the scope of AI-supported instructional design
target_learners: K-12 and higher education teachers acting as instructional designers
target_learning_goals: Design of effective, equitable, and adaptive learning tasks with AI support
examples: Figure 5 presents a function-affordance matrix showing which of the 28 reviewed studies reported each function-affordance pairing, with creativity and equity tied to a broader range of AI features than efficiency and responsiveness.
key_sources: Zongran Wang, Liu Mingzhuo & A.Y.M. Atiquil Islam. (2026). Reimagining teacher-AI co-design in learning task design: trends and perspectives. HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES COMMUNICATIONS. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06981-y

article_title: Transcription is not generation: Distinguishing non-generative AI tool use from academic misconduct in higher education assessment
citation: Craig Wright. (2026). Transcription is not generation: distinguishing non-generative AI tool use from academic misconduct in higher education assessment. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00234-w
title: Assess AI use by the function performed, not the platform used
description: The paper argues that academic integrity judgements should turn on which AI function was performed rather than which platform was used: 'The question for academic integrity purposes, on the view defended here, is not 'which platform was used?' but 'which function was performed?'' Multi-functional platforms possess both generative and non-generative capabilities, so platform identity cannot determine whether a prohibition is engaged. The principle is argued to be implicit in existing institutional practice with grammar checkers and dictation software.
requirements: If an institution's position is that any interaction with any platform possessing generative capabilities constitutes prohibited use, the paper argues that such a position must be stated explicitly
constraints: The paper acknowledges some institutions do restrict tools like Grammarly and makes no claim about universal practice
The paper does not claim to have systematically surveyed every institutional policy
target_learners: higher education students
faculty and misconduct panel members
target_learning_goals: fair application of academic integrity policy
examples: The paper argues a student using a platform solely for OCR transcription of handwritten work into LaTeX has not used the generative function, so a 'generative AI' prohibition is not engaged
key_sources: Craig Wright. (2026). Transcription is not generation: distinguishing non-generative AI tool use from academic misconduct in higher education assessment. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00234-w

article_title:
THE ROBUSTNESS OF CRITICAL PERIOD EFFECTS IN SECOND LANGUAGE
ACQUISITION
citation: Robert M. DeKeyser. (2000). THE ROBUSTNESS OF CRITICAL PERIOD EFFECTS IN SECOND LANGUAGE ACQUISITION. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 22, Issue 4. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100004022
title: Fundamental Difference Hypothesis: adults lose implicit domain-specific language learning mechanisms and rely on problem-solving capacities
description: The Fundamental Difference Hypothesis (Bley-Vroman, 1988) holds that children learn language almost completely through implicit domain-specific mechanisms, whereas adults have largely lost the ability to learn a language without reflecting on its structure. Adults must instead use alternative mechanisms, "drawing especially on their problem-solving capacities, to learn a second language." The article tests this hypothesis empirically with adult immigrants.
requirements: The hypothesis implies that only adults with a high level of verbal analytical ability will reach near-native competence in their second language.
target_learners: adult second language learners
examples: The study tested the hypothesis with 57 adult Hungarian-speaking immigrants using a grammaticality judgment test.

article_title: Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1)
citation: Kearney CA, Gonzálvez C, Graczyk PA and Fornander MJ (2019) Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1). Front. Psychol. 10:2222. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02222
title: Functional model of school attendance problems with four maintaining functions
description: Kearney and colleagues' functional model focuses on variables that maintain or reinforce school attendance problems, designed primarily for Tier 2-type, child-initiated problems. The postulated functions are refusal to attend school to (1) avoid school-based stimuli provoking negative affectivity, (2) escape aversive social and/or evaluative situations, (3) seek attention from significant others, and/or (4) pursue tangible rewards outside of school. The first two reflect negative reinforcement and the latter two positive reinforcement.
requirements: A profile of the relative strength of each functional condition is recommended during case analysis
constraints: Designed primarily as a clinical approach for Tier 2-type school attendance problems, particularly child-initiated attendance problems
target_learners: children and adolescents with child-initiated school attendance problems
target_learning_goals: matching prescriptive treatment packages to the function of a student's attendance problem
examples: The model links to prescriptive treatment packages adapted across educational, mental health, and medical settings

article_title: Finding and using students’ funds of knowledge and identity in superdiverse primary schools: a collaborative action research project
citation: J. 't Gilde, M. Volman. (2021). Finding and using students’ funds of knowledge and identity in superdiverse primary schools: a collaborative action research project. Cambridge Journal of Education, 51(6), 673-692. https://doi.org/10.1080/0305764X.2021.1906845
title: Funds of knowledge/identity theory: building on skills and knowledge students acquire in families, communities and peer groups
description: Funds of knowledge/identity (FoK/I) theory is an explanatory framework holding that students acquire skills and knowledge in their families, communities and peer groups that teachers may fail to recognise, particularly across sociocultural difference. The article states that the theory "makes a plea for building on the skills and knowledge that students acquire in their families, communities and peer groups". It is used as the theoretical basis for a collaborative action research project on teaching in superdiverse primary classrooms.
requirements: Teachers must be able to recognise skills and knowledge students acquire outside school that may otherwise go unrecognised.
constraints: The article frames the theory as relevant where teachers and students are from different sociocultural backgrounds in superdiverse classrooms.
target_learners: primary school students in superdiverse classrooms
target_learning_goals: building instruction on students' family, community and peer-group knowledge and skills
examples: The authors used FoK/I theory to frame a collaborative action research project investigating how primary school teachers can use students' FoK/I in their classrooms.

article_title: Metacognitive emotion regulation: Children's awareness that changing thoughts and goals can alleviate negative emotions.
citation: Davis, E. L., Levine, L. J., Lench, H. C., & Quas, J. A. (2010). Metacognitive Emotion Regulation: Children’s Awareness that Changing Thoughts and Goals Can Alleviate Negative Emotions. Emotion, 10(4), 498–510. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018428
title: Functionalist appraisal account linking discrete emotions to goal-status change and distinct regulation strategies
description: The article adopts a functionalist model in which "people experience emotions when the status of a goal has changed." Anger arises when a goal is obstructed but reinstatement seems possible and motivates action against obstacles; sadness reflects irrevocable goal failure; fear reflects threatened but not yet occurred goal failure. The authors used this account to predict which regulation strategies children would report for each emotion, and the Study 2 pattern was consistent with it.
requirements: Predicting strategy–emotion matches requires knowing the appraisal profile (goal status) of the specific emotion
constraints: The article notes future research must test whether event controllability, which was not manipulated, also shapes children's strategy selection
target_learners: 5- and 6-year-old children
target_learning_goals: emotion regulation and coping with negative emotions
examples: Children reported changing goals most often for sad events such as a pet's death, where the goal cannot be reinstated, and changing thoughts for frightening events such as a monster under the bed.
key_sources: Davis, E. L., Levine, L. J., Lench, H. C., & Quas, J. A. (2010). Metacognitive Emotion Regulation: Children’s Awareness that Changing Thoughts and Goals Can Alleviate Negative Emotions. Emotion, 10(4), 498–510. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018428

article_title: Future technology workshop: A collaborative method for the design of new learning technologies and activities
citation: Giasemi N. Vavoula and Mike Sharples. (2007). Future Technology Workshop: A Collaborative Method for the Design of New Learning Technologies and Activities. Pre-print, to appear in International Journal of Computer Supported Collaborative Learning, Volume 2, Issue 4, December 2007. https://www.ftw.org.uk
title: The Future Technology Workshop method for envisioning future technology-activity systems
description: The Future Technology Workshop (FTW) is a structured participatory method in which participants with everyday knowledge of a domain envision and design interactions between current and future technology and activity. It organises this exploration as a four-box grid crossing current/future activity with current/future technology, and runs seven sessions: Imagineering, Modelling, Role-play, Retrofit, Everyday, Futurefit and Requirements. The aim is "to reach an informed understanding of how people might interact with technology in the future (box 4 in Table #2) by exploring the possibilities represented by all four boxes".
requirements: Participants familiar with the domain of interest but not generally technology experts
Two or three facilitators managing and recording the sessions
A large room with cheap and portable low-tech prototyping materials
constraints: Targets primarily the Exploratory Design stage of new-generation product design, i.e. product conception
target_learners: children and adults with everyday domain knowledge participating in technology design workshops
target_learning_goals: envisioning future technology-supported activities and specifying requirements for new learning technologies
examples: Used with children and adults to explore new technology-activity systems including interacting with digital photographs and informal science learning
key_sources: Giasemi N. Vavoula and Mike Sharples. (2007). Future Technology Workshop: A Collaborative Method for the Design of New Learning Technologies and Activities. article_title: Collaboration scripts and scaffolding
citation: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Carolyn P. Rosé, & Gerry Stahl. (2016). Collaboration scripts and scaffolding. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 11, 381–385. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9247-1
title: Functional system incorporating tools as the unit of analysis for CSCL microanalysis
description: Arnseth and Krange argue, building on Vygotsky and Wertsch, that "the unit of analysis needs to be a functional system incorporating tools." This stance opens up understanding of the multiplicity of activities, in which collaboration between students and computational tools can take multiple paths, and analysts must understand how participants orient themselves through a series of activities and why they choose specific paths. The editors present it as grounding ethnographic description combined with detailed turn-by-turn interaction analysis of upper-secondary students' inquiry into energy phenomena.
requirements: Multi-level analysis combining ethnographic description and detailed micro-analysis of interaction over time
constraints: The account is framed for naturalistic educational settings such as schools, where the teacher plays an important role
target_learners: upper-secondary school students working on inquiry problems in science
target_learning_goals: understanding phenomena of energy and energy transformation through collaborative inquiry
examples: Arnseth and Krange study how upper-secondary students try to understand energy and energy transformation, with teachers as part of the activities
key_sources: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Carolyn P. Rosé, & Gerry Stahl. (2016). Collaboration scripts and scaffolding. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 11, 381–385. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9247-1

article_title: Students’ multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment
citation: Anu Kajamaa & Kristiina Kumpulainen. (2020). Students' multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2020) 15:411–444. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09337-z
title: FUSE Studio makerspace with 30 self-selected STEAM challenges and leveling difficulty
description: The FUSE Studio is a school-based makerspace concept, originally created at Northwestern University, consisting of "a computer program and hands-on material packages including 30 (pre-given) activities, called challenges". Students freely choose a challenge, partners (or working alone), and pace, via the "My Challenges" web interface with trailer videos. Challenges range from jewelry design to 3D-modelled dream homes, windmills, solar-powered cars, laser mazes and roller coasters, and "level up in difficulty following the basic logic of video game design principles". Assessment is ungraded, using photos, video, digital artifacts and student documentation.
requirements: Digital tools (computers, 3D printers), hands-on material kits, a website providing challenge instructions, and teacher facilitation, with teachers making rounds in the space
constraints: Some challenges are fully digital while others use provided physical kits; teachers do not need advanced digital competence, since FUSE offers low-threshold activity
target_learners: Elementary students (ages 9–12) in elective courses; concept also adopted in other Finnish schools
target_learning_goals: STEAM learning, creative problem solving, collaboration and digital competence through interest-driven design and making
examples: In the study school, students used the computer lab, a neighboring classroom and the corridor for challenges such as building a laser security system for a 'treasure'.

article_title: Futurising science education: students’ experiences from a course on futures thinking and quantum computing
citation: Tapio Rasa, Elina Palmgren, Antti Laherto. (2022). Futurising science education: students' experiences from a course on futures thinking and quantum computing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09572-3
title: Futures thinking connected to the projective dimension of transformative agency
description: The article frames futures thinking — the ability of "disengaging from deterministic future views, understanding the plurality of futures and identifying and questioning assumptions to develop alternative scenarios" — as deeply influencing agency, defined as the capacity for intentional transformative action. Building on Emirbayer and Mische, the projective dimension of agency links futures thinking to transformative agency because it denotes imagining alternatives free from constraining schemas. The framework maps probable, possible and preferable futures onto agentic dimensions and motivates visioning and backcasting in science education.
requirements: Teaching should engage students in building alternative scenarios and questioning assumptions for the projective dimension to be exercised
constraints: The article focuses on upper-secondary science education contexts and on individual students' takes on futures and agency, while also attending to social aspects
target_learners: upper-secondary school students
examples: The course used the Futures Cone, scenario building across probable, possible and preferable futures, and backcasting from preferable futures
key_sources: Tapio Rasa, Elina Palmgren, Antti Laherto. (2022). Futurising science education: students' experiences from a course on futures thinking and quantum computing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09572-3

article_title: Futurising science education: students’ experiences from a course on futures thinking and quantum computing
citation: Tapio Rasa, Elina Palmgren, Antti Laherto. (2022). Futurising science education: students' experiences from a course on futures thinking and quantum computing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09572-3
title: Future-oriented science course combining authentic emerging technology with futures-studies methods
description: A lesson/course-level design in which a contemporary science topic (quantum computing) provides continuity from scientific knowledge to emerging technologies and their future possibilities, intertwined with futures-studies methods. "Students were guided to employ, by turns, three fundamentally different types of thinking methods commonly used in futures studies: probable, possible and preferable futures", followed by a backcasting exercise in which students imagine themselves as active participants in reaching a preferable future. Group projects on personally chosen socio-scientific problems run throughout the module, supported by the Futures Cone visualisation and systems thinking tools.
requirements: A science topic offering continuity from accessible scientific knowledge to emerging technology and future possibilities
sustained group project work on a personally relevant socio-scientific problem
constraints: The module was implemented as an extra-curricular course of about 20 hours with STEM-specialisation students
target_learners: upper-secondary school students in STEM specialisation programmes
examples: Two course weekends plus an evening session; students used a real publicly available IBM quantum processor; final presentations were success stories told in past tense
key_sources: Tapio Rasa, Elina Palmgren, Antti Laherto. (2022). Futurising science education: students' experiences from a course on futures thinking and quantum computing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09572-3

article_title: Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design
citation: Charlott Sellberg & Oskar Lindwall. (2025). Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09763-2
title: Design simulations for functional correspondence with the task elements most consequential for professional performance, matched to learner stage
description: The editorial recommends that simulation design, rather than replicating reality wholesale, focus on identifying and preserving the task elements most consequential for professional performance — motor routines, critical decisions, and forms of coordination — presented in ways appropriate to the learner's developmental stage. Functional resemblance is treated as "a design hypothesis – something to be tested, adapted, and refined in situ". Simplified or deliberately inauthentic setups may be pedagogically superior for novices.
requirements: Designers must identify which task elements — motor routines, critical decisions, forms of coordination — are most consequential for professional performance
constraints: Overly authentic environments may impede novice learning by demanding too many interacting elements before essentials are mastered; what counts as correspondence varies by domain, learner stage, and pedagogical purpose
target_learners: novices through advanced learners in professional education
target_learning_goals: professional performance skills, decision-making, and coordination
examples: Forestry teachers intentionally simplify simulator tasks to enable volume training of key manoeuvres, reconnecting them later to broader professional trajectories through discussion and fieldwork
key_sources: Charlott Sellberg & Oskar Lindwall. (2025). Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09763-2

article_title: Technology-Supported Interventions and Learners’ Metacognition: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
citation: Yijia Yuan & Yiran Du. (2026). Technology-Supported Interventions and Learners' Metacognition: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10227-3
title: Functional framework of technology-supported metacognitive scaffolding across four regulatory processes
description: The article frames technology-supported metacognitive interventions functionally: scaffolds embedded in prompts, dashboards, portfolios, diaries, adaptive feedback, and conversational tools support four regulatory processes — planning, monitoring, evaluation/reflection, and strategic control. It argues "the relevant distinction is therefore not only the technology used but the regulatory activity its features are intended to support", so technological category alone may not fully explain intervention effectiveness. AI systems extend this repertoire by making support more adaptive, with roles ranging from directing learning to augmenting learner decision-making.
requirements: A process is coded as supported only when the intervention explicitly supports it, not merely from outcome instruments, theoretical framing, or automated system adaptivity
constraints: The article notes extensive system control may reduce opportunities for learners to practise independent regulation, and that capable systems can perform regulatory work on learners' behalf, raising questions about learner agency
target_learners: K–12 and post-secondary students in formal educational settings
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive planning, monitoring, evaluation/reflection, and strategic control during learning
examples: The review coded each of the 33 included interventions for which of the four regulatory-support processes its features explicitly represented, producing a study-level evidence map (Table 1)
key_sources: Yijia Yuan & Yiran Du. (2026). Technology-Supported Interventions and Learners' Metacognition: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10227-3

article_title: How Future Goals Enhance Motivation and Learning in Multicultural Classrooms
citation: Phalet, K., Andriessen, I., & Lens, W. (2004). How Future Goals Enhance Motivation and Learning in Multicultural Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review, Vol. 16, No. 1. https://hdl.handle.net/1874/23520
title: Future time perspective theory: cognitive (instrumentality) and dynamic (incentive value) aspects connecting present task goals to distant future goals
description: The review's organizing motivational framework, drawn from Nuttin and Lens (1985) and De Volder and Lens (1982), holds that formulating goals in the distant future creates an extended future time perspective (FTP) that strengthens goal striving. The theory distinguishes two aspects: "the cognitive aspect of FTP refers to the instrumentality or utility value of immediate task goals to reach distant future goals, the dynamic aspect concerns the incentive value of more or less distant future goals." A longer FTP raises perceived utility of schoolwork and reduces the steepness of incentive discounting of delayed rewards. The review applies this framework to explain when future goals motivate minority students.
requirements: Distinguishing immediate task goals from delayed future goals
Perceived positive connections between present tasks and future goals
constraints: The effect of FTP extension on incentive value is curvilinear, smaller for goals in the very near or very distant future than for goals in the intermediate future
target_learners: secondary and vocational school students, including minority students in multicultural classrooms
target_learning_goals: achievement motivation, learning strategy use, and school performance
examples: De Volder and Lens (1982) found a positive correlation between Grade 11 students' total motivation and the length of their FTP; Creten et al. (2001) found positive correlations between perceived instrumentality of theoretical and practical courses and motivation in vocational schools
key_sources: Phalet, K., Andriessen, I., & Lens, W. (2004). How Future Goals Enhance Motivation and Learning in Multicultural Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review, Vol. 16, No. 1. https://hdl.handle.net/1874/23520

article_title: Interactivity in Video-based Models
citation: Wouters, P., Tabbers, H. K., & Paas, F. (2007). Interactivity in Video-based Models. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 327–342. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9045-4
title: Two-level model of interactivity: functional and cognitive interactivity
description: Adopting Kennedy's (2004) model, the review distinguishes two levels of interactivity centered on instructional events. "The first level, functional interactivity, comprises the behavioral responses learners engage in when they face an instructional event," while the second level, cognitive interactivity, proposes that these behavioral responses mediate between instructional events and (meta)cognitive processes. The review argues guidelines for interactivity should address both components, and that clicking a button without the purpose of eliciting desired cognitive processes is not interaction relevant for learning.
requirements: Guidelines must describe both the behavioral actions addressed and the cognitive processes they mediate
constraints: The effect of an instructional event and its behavioral response may depend on factors outside interactivity itself, most importantly prior knowledge
target_learners: learners in electronic learning environments
target_learning_goals: engaging learners in cognitive and metacognitive processes during interaction with learning materials
examples: A prediction prompt is functional interactivity (answering a question) whose behavioral response may trigger selection, organization and integration of information with prior knowledge
key_sources: Wouters, P., Tabbers, H. K., & Paas, F. (2007). Interactivity in Video-based Models. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 327–342. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9045-4

article_title: When Fine is Large and Gross is Small: A Meta-Analysis of Links Between Fine and Gross Motor Skills with Academic-Cognitive Skills
citation: Karle, V. L., Suggate, S. P., Winter, R., & Stoeger, H. (2026). When Fine is Large and Gross is Small: A Meta-Analysis of Links Between Fine and Gross Motor Skills with Academic-Cognitive Skills. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10161-4
title: Functionalism and shared action-cognition accounts of motor–academic-cognitive links
description: The article organizes theoretical explanations for motor–academic-cognitive associations into two perspectives. Functionalism holds that "children with better motor skills can more easily access and engage in learning opportunities", including writing facilitating reading and lower cognitive load in combined motor-cognitive tasks. The shared action-cognition account holds that academic-cognitive skills "share and can recruit motor networks during task performance" (e.g., handwriting networks during reading, finger perception networks during mathematics). The authors state the two perspectives "are not necessarily mutually exclusive" and use both to interpret the FiMS advantage.
requirements: Both perspectives are used to interpret correlational evidence; the article notes experimental evidence for a functional mechanism exists mainly for older children (motor skills facilitating writing, which improves reading).
constraints: The meta-analysis is correlational, so these accounts are interpretations rather than tested mechanisms; the article notes the lack of an age moderating effect makes one functionalist exploration-based explanation unlikely for middle childhood and adolescence.
target_learners: children and adolescents aged 3–16 in typical (non-clinical) samples
target_learning_goals: academic skills (reading, writing, mathematics, language, general attainment)
examples: The discussion reads the stronger FiMS associations as support for functionalism's emphasis on engaging with learning materials and dealing with fine motor demands of school tasks, while also invoking shared neural activation between motor and cognitive areas.
key_sources: Karle, V. L., Suggate, S. P., Winter, R., & Stoeger, H. (2026). When Fine is Large and Gross is Small: A Meta-Analysis of Links Between Fine and Gross Motor Skills with Academic-Cognitive Skills. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10161-4

article_title: Watch Your Step Children! Learning Two-Digit Numbers Through Mirror-Based Observation of Self-Initiated Body Movements
citation: Margina Ruiter & Sofie Loyens & Fred Paas. (2015). Watch Your Step Children! Learning Two-Digit Numbers Through Mirror-Based Observation of Self-Initiated Body Movements. Educ Psychol Rev (2015) 27:457–474. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9324-4
title: Integrate task-related full-body movements into conventional math number building exercises because they improve performance at low cost
description: The principle is to embed meaningful, task-related full-body movements into standard math exercises: children build two-digit numbers by making steps of different sizes along a floor ruler, with "tens were represented by large steps, fives by mediate, and ones by very small steps", while verbalizing the count. The article argues this improves performance over the predominant sit-and-write method and fits the trend toward more physical activity in primary schools.
requirements: A floor ruler with marks indicating ones, fives, and tens, and exercises in which step size is proportionate to the number units being built
constraints: The article cautions that one must be careful drawing educational-practice conclusions from a single study; the specific active ingredient of the movements could not be determined from the design
target_learners: first-grade elementary school children learning two-digit numbers
target_learning_goals: numerical concept understanding: positioning of numbers on a number line, number magnitude, and number structure
examples: In the experiment, children in movement conditions construed numbers like 36 by saying 10, 20, 30, 35, 36 while making three big steps, one medium, and one small step on a 3.2 m ruler across the gym floor
key_sources: Margina Ruiter & Sofie Loyens & Fred Paas. (2015). Watch Your Step Children! Learning Two-Digit Numbers Through Mirror-Based Observation of Self-Initiated Body Movements. Educ Psychol Rev (2015) 27:457–474. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9324-4

article_title: Resilience research in learning disabilities: Guiding principles from developmental psychopathology
citation: Slomowitz R. F., Narayan A. J., & McGrath L. M. (2025). Resilience research in learning disabilities: Guiding principles from developmental psychopathology. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102090
title: Study academic resilience with tests of both main and interaction effects embedded in a full 2×2 risk-by-resilience-factor design
description: The paper's central methodological recommendation is that analyses of resilience in LD research must include "a statistical test of main and interaction effects" and "the full 2 × 2 conceptual matrix of presence/absence of a suspected resilience factor and high/low risk groups" (HR+, HR−, LR+, LR−) to determine gap-maintaining versus gap-closing effects. Without the low-risk group divided by factor presence, interactions cannot be tested and promotive versus protective status cannot be determined.
requirements: Sufficient numbers of individuals in the lower-risk/non-LD group both with and without the resilience factor of interest when applying the matrix to pre-existing datasets
Careful investigation and plotting of interaction forms, since a significant interaction is not necessarily protective
constraints: The matrix can be applied categorically or dimensionally, with risk status and resilience factor entered as continuous main effects and interaction terms
target_learners: children at risk for learning disabilities
children with learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: identifying promotive and protective factors for academic outcomes
examples: Slomowitz et al. (2021) used dimensional measurement of risk and resilience factors with a categorical follow-up of the interaction to show vocabulary was promotive but not protective
key_sources: Slomowitz R. F., Narayan A. J., & McGrath L. M. (2025). Resilience research in learning disabilities: Guiding principles from developmental psychopathology. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102090

article_title: Pupils' estimates of teachers.
citation: Grace E. Bird. (1917). Pupils' Estimates of Teachers. Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Teachers should endeavor to fulfil the requirements of both supervisor and pupil, since pupils appreciate the ordinary virtues fundamental to character.
description: The article argues that because employers and supervisors "are forced to rely upon appearances" and can rarely observe instructors' work, while pupils possess intimate daily acquaintance with teachers, the effective teacher should satisfy both audiences' criteria. It concludes "it behooves the instructor of youth to endeavor to fulfil all the requirements of both supervisor and pupil." Pupils' lists emphasize social-character virtues, and the author argues the parallelism between the two lists is closer than it seems because loose general terms hide similar ideas.
requirements: The teacher must be evaluated by both supervisor criteria (instructional skill, discipline, initiative, experience) and pupil criteria (kindness, fairness, sociability, humor and related virtues).
constraints: The article notes pupils appreciate most "the ordinary virtues fundamental to character," and that standardized methods of rating teachers' fitness are often absent.
target_learners: high school students
normal school students
examples: The study collected unsigned written answers from 139 high school girls, 253 high school boys, and 150 normal school students naming the best qualities of their best teachers, then compared these with employers' qualification lists and documented causes of teacher failure.
key_sources: Grace E. Bird. (1917). Pupils' Estimates of Teachers. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072302

article_title: Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience
citation: Robert Colvin. (2016). Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.12
title: Functional activation signatures as the measurement focus: brain activity before, during and after learning
description: The article defines functional activation signatures as temporally staged patterns of brain activity in which 'activity takes place mostly in sensory processing areas before becoming more dominant in areas associated with higher-order cognitive abilities'. It argues the neuroscientific focus should be on brain activity before, during and after learning a task, rather than on task performance, since learning indicates a physical change in the brain such as synaptic plasticity, neurogenesis, or changes in neurons, in grey matter, white matter or both.
requirements: Measurement technology able to capture temporal and spatial changes in brain activity across days or weeks
constraints: Neuroscientific knowledge remains limited by the complexity of the brain and technological and financial constraints of current tools
target_learners: learners undergoing instructional interventions
target_learning_goals: relating brain change to academic attainment
examples: Comparing activation signatures between novice and expert on a geometry task to locate bottlenecks

article_title: Lab perceptual training and robot-assisted training in improving speech prosody of autistic children
citation: Chen, S., Wang, B.X., Cheung, J.C.-W. et al. (2026). Lab perceptual training and robot-assisted training in improving speech prosody of autistic children. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00425-7
title: Furhat robot-assisted speech training system with simulated social interaction
description: The system uses the social robot Furhat, which "can be programmed to interact with autistic children and provide effective training", with cloud-based speech recognition (Google ASR and Microsoft Azure Cognitive Services) and speech synthesis (Amazon Polly and Acapela TTS), a back-projected face with synchronized lip movements, and face tracking. A web-application architecture (Raspberry Pi 4B web server in Golang, React.js GUI with participant and instructor modes) synchronizes image display, audio and the robot's facial expressions. Children ask the robot questions and judge whether its answers match the elicited focus type and position.
requirements: A Furhat robot with cloud-based ASR and TTS services, a slim client with an internet browser, and the custom web server and GUI system for interaction control and synchronization
constraints: Training materials were limited to six sentences with subject-verb-object structure; the study's sentences were limited to five-syllable subject-verb-object structures
target_learners: Cantonese-speaking autistic children
target_learning_goals: Using prosodic cues (duration, f0, intensity) to mark broad, narrow and contrastive focus in speech production
examples: In training phase one, participants asked the robot questions eliciting focus and identified focus position and type by clicking buttons while the robot answered with congruent, matched prosody

article_title: Towards Designing Profitable Courses: Predicting Student Purchasing Behaviour in MOOCs
citation: Alshehri, M., Alamri, A., Cristea, A. I., & Stewart, C. D. (2021). Towards Designing Profitable Courses: Predicting Student Purchasing Behaviour in MOOCs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 215–233. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00246-2
title: FutureLearn multi-run MOOC dataset (23 runs, 5 courses, 245,255 learners) with clickstream and demographic features
description: A large-scale dataset of 23 runs spread over 5 University of Warwick courses delivered via FutureLearn between 2013 and 2017, spanning literature, psychology, computer science and business. It combines system-logged clickstream activity (3,007,789 materials accessed; 2,794,578 steps declared completed) with optional survey demographics (gender, age group, education level, country, employment status and area). The derived time-spent feature is computed as the difference between first visit and last completion timestamps per step. The authors state it covers "a total of 23 runs spread over 5 MOOC courses, on 4 distinct topic areas".
requirements: Learners' optional demographic survey responses and system logs correlating unique IDs and timestamps to learner activities
constraints: Analysing a single platform, FutureLearn, which the authors state limits the work
target_learners: MOOC learners on FutureLearn, predominantly professional, highly educated adults from developed nations
target_learning_goals: Predicting certificate purchasing decisions and course revenue in online courses
examples: Courses analysed: Shakespeare and his World (10 weeks), The Mind is Flat (6 weeks), Babies in Mind (4 weeks), Big Data (9 weeks), Supply Chains (6 weeks)

article_title: Functional Technology for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities: Meta-Analysis of Mobile Device-Based Interventions
citation: Jemma Kim & Christina H. Kimm. (2017). Functional Technology for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities: Meta-Analysis of Mobile Device-Based Interventions. The Journal of Special Education Apprenticeship, 6(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Functional+Technology+for+Individuals+with+Intellectual+Disabilities+Meta-Analysis+of+Mobile+Device-Based+Interventions
title: Functional Technology (FT) as a new paradigm beyond assistive technology for people with intellectual disabilities
description: The article proposes functional technology as a paradigm in which people with intellectual disabilities proficiently use mainstream technology, including mobile devices, in daily activities and various environments, beyond specialized assistive technology. It defines FT as "the process of implementing any assistive technology in daily routines, managing and navigating the network, and manipulating software that addresses the specific needs of individual with disabilities" (Kimm, 2016). The authors argue FT supports social integration and normalization because mobile devices' universal handheld design minimizes focus on the user's disability.
requirements: Access to mainstream mobile devices and appropriate apps and internet resources
Support for people with ID to become active agents in learning and implementing functional technology rather than passive recipients of instruction
constraints: Research on mobile device effectiveness beyond instructional technology in the classroom is described as being in a beginning stage
target_learners: individuals with intellectual disabilities
students with developmental disabilities
examples: Uphold et al. (2016) instructed six adults with ID to schedule exercising routines using an ePAS app on an iPod Touch; Kelley et al. (2013) used picture prompts on iPod to teach four young adults with ID campus navigation, with generalization to various locations

article_title: Evaluating the Promise of the "FUSION" Tier 2 Math Intervention
citation: Strand Cary, M., Doabler, C., Clarke, B., Fien, H., Baker, S. K., & Jungjohann, K. (2013). Evaluating the Promise of the FUSION Tier 2 Math Intervention. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: FUSION: a Grade 1 Tier 2 whole-number mathematics intervention with four content strands and 60 scripted explicit lessons
description: FUSION is a Grade 1 Tier 2 mathematics intervention focused on "building students' early knowledge of whole number concepts." It comprises four math strands — base-10/place value, basic number combinations, multi-digit addition and subtraction without renaming, and word problems — delivered through 60 scripted lessons in an explicit instructional format. Lessons run about 30 minutes in small groups of roughly 4-5 students, three times per week, outside core math and reading time.
requirements: Delivered by trained interventionists outside core math and reading time, one lesson per day three times per week
constraints: Designed for Grade 1 students at risk for mathematics difficulties who speak English, regularly attend school, and can identify and count from 1-10
target_learners: Grade 1 students at risk for mathematics difficulties
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of whole number concepts and skills
Procedural fluency with early number operations
examples: Lessons contain teacher modeling, scaffolded instructional examples, and opportunities for academic feedback, with frequent student practice and judicious review

citation: Strand Cary, M., Doabler, C., Clarke, B., Fien, H., Baker, S. K., & Jungjohann, K. (2013). Evaluating the Promise of the FUSION Tier 2 Math Intervention. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Explicit instructional lesson format combining teacher modeling, scaffolded examples, academic feedback, practice, and review
description: The FUSION lessons instantiate an explicit instructional design pattern: "Lessons contain teacher modeling, scaffolded instructional examples, and opportunities for academic feedback." Lessons also "incorporate a variety of math models and offer frequent opportunities for student practice and judicious review." Observers documented presence or absence of these design principles per activity to compute implementation fidelity.
requirements: Interventionists implement the specified design principles (e.g., models the skill or concept, provides group response opportunities, provides academic feedback) for fidelity
constraints: Scripted lessons of approximately 30 minutes in small-group format of approximately 4-5 students
target_learners: First-grade students at risk for mathematics difficulties in small intervention groups
target_learning_goals: Whole number concepts and procedural fluency
examples: Fidelity was calculated as the percentage of design principles implemented across the 4-5 activities per lesson, with an overall 7-point fidelity rating

title: Multi-step at-risk screening process using brief EN-CBM number-sense measures plus teacher recommendation
description: FUSION-eligible students were identified through a multi-step screening process of all first graders conducted three months into the school year. Brief EN-CBM number-sense measures were administered to identify students with the lowest mathematics performance, and need was further verified by teacher recommendation and rating of classroom mathematics performance. Eligibility additionally required speaking English, regular attendance, and the ability to identify and count numbers 1-10.
requirements: Brief measures of number sense (EN-CBM) administered to all first graders in each participating school
Teacher recommendation and performance rating to verify need
constraints: Screening occurred three months into the school year; students had to speak English, regularly attend school, identify numbers 1-10, and count from 1-10
target_learners: First graders screened for mathematics difficulty risk
target_learning_goals: Early identification of students needing Tier 2 whole-number intervention
examples: At each school, identified at-risk students were randomly assigned to FUSION or at-risk control, with about five students per condition per school

citation: Strand Cary, M., Doabler, C., Clarke, B., Fien, H., Baker, S. K., & Jungjohann, K. (2013). Evaluating the Promise of the FUSION Tier 2 Math Intervention. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Outcome and observation measurement suite: proximal and distal math measures plus fidelity and instructional-quality observation instruments
description: The pilot measures conceptual understanding and procedural fluency with both proximal and distal outcomes: modified and unmodified EN-CBM subtests, SAT-10 problem solving and procedures subtests, and the researcher-developed ProFUSION assessment of FUSION content for at-risk conditions. Instruction is observed with the FUSION observation instrument, which measures implementation fidelity, and the RCMIS, which rates 11 features of instructional quality across learning environment, classroom management, and delivery of instruction on a 4-point scale.

title: Full Code Medical Simulation platform
description: Full Code is a virtual simulation software by Minerva Medical, an internet-independent platform offering more than 150 realistic clinical cases for practicing clinical reasoning. Each completed case yields an automatically generated performance report that "assigns a score based on three weighted components: correct diagnosis (35%), correct disposition (20%), and individual actions taken (45%)", with actions categorized as critical, recommended, neutral, unnecessary or harmful. In this study instructors encouraged its voluntary use as a supplementary tool aligned to course learning objectives.

title: Align simulator fidelity with learners' needs and key tasks rather than maximizing physical realism
description: Drawing on Hamstra et al., the article argues that higher perceived fidelity does not necessarily improve educational outcomes unless it aligns with learners' needs and objectives; "functional fidelity—or alignment of key tasks—may be more critical for promoting the effective transfer of skills." Accordingly, elements like vibration and noise were included in MeTra to mirror essential facets of HEMS operations while balancing authenticity with educational benefit, since high physical fidelity may impose excessive cognitive load on novices.
requirements: Identify the key tasks of the target operational environment and reproduce those facets in the simulator
constraints: The article states further analysis is needed to identify whether novices risk being overwhelmed by high physical fidelity

target_learning_goals: Effective transfer of trained skills to real operational settings

title: LLM-enhanced social robotic virtual patient platform (Furhat robot with OpenAI gpt-3.5-turbo)
description: A virtual patient presentation platform combining the Furhat social robot with the OpenAI gpt-3.5-turbo language model. The robot has "an animated face and a neck that allows realistic head movements" and displays subtle facial expressions and gaze behaviour; the LLM was prompted to select facial expressions at anchor points and generated patient responses from a detailed patient description plus the last 10 dialogue turns. An LED turn-holding cue signalled whether the robot was perceiving input or about to respond.
requirements: A detailed patient description embedded in the LLM prompt to prevent assistant-like phrasings
A turn-holding cue (LED light) to avoid misinterpretation of when it is possible to talk to the VP
constraints: The platform as used offered no physical examination or laboratory testing options, and response delays sometimes caused interruptions
target_learners: third-year medical students
examples: Ten VP cases covering rheumatic conditions such as RA, PMR, gout, SLE, GPA, dermatomyositis and spondyloarthritis were presented on this platform and a computer-based VIC simulator
